clue.text: Standing charges for donjon support?

definitions.meaning: regular running costs that must be met
a donjon is a castle keep, and its maintenance is literally the care of a keep

explanation.surface: A question about who pays the regular costs of holding up a castle tower.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as a phrase: keeping a keep, or donjon, in repair.
explanation.definitionFit: Maintenance costs are a fixed, recurring outlay, the classic standing charge.

clue.text: Townsman I pop out and upset

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and tumbled, so the letters of the words around are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A town dweller pops out for a moment and is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges I POP and AND; 'out' is a link word. An Oppidan is an Eton College boy boarding in the town rather than in college.
explanation.definitionFit: Oppidan comes from Latin oppidum, a town, and means an inhabitant of a town.

clue.text: The relic a fabrication, contrary to popular belief

indicators.note: a fabrication is something made up, so these letters are reassembled into a new word

explanation.surface: Someone claims a holy relic is fake, against what everyone believes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabrication' signals a rearrangement of THE RELIC A.
explanation.definitionFit: Heresy is opinion opposed to orthodox doctrine, so a heretical view goes against accepted belief.

clue.text: From which an academician takes a draught in the bistro

definitions.text: From which an academician takes a draught in the bistro

indicators.note: in places the Academy member inside the word for the bistro

parts.note: a bistro is a small cafe
RA stands for Royal Academician

explanation.surface: An artist from the Royal Academy sips a drink at a French bistro.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Academy of Arts is London's academy of painters; the whole clue also describes the vessel a drink is poured from, so it reads as both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine bottle-shaped glass jug from which drinks are poured at table.

clue.text: Crazy gunmen somewhere East of Suez

parts.note: crazy means mad
RA is the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners, so men of the RA are RAs

explanation.surface: Wild gunmen roam a distant land beyond the canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gunmen' looks like armed criminals but means members of the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: Madras, now Chennai, is an Indian city, well east of the Suez Canal.

clue.text: Expensive wood ex-Open champion Ben may take round

indicators.note: take round means the word may wraps itself about the golfer's surname

parts.note: taken as written
Ben Hogan won the Open golf championship in 1953

explanation.surface: A former golf champion is taken on a tour around the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take round' means one piece encloses the other; 'may' looks like a verb of possibility but is simply the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense reddish tropical hardwood prized and costly for fine furniture.

clue.text: Largely drank up a store of supplies

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the letters are read from the bottom upwards
largely means most of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily, so drank is toped

explanation.surface: Someone has drunk most of the stock in a supply store.
explanation.walkthrough: TOPED A, with 'Largely' dropping its final A, is read upwards ('up') to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a warehouse or storehouse where goods and supplies are kept.

clue.text: Sailors in the drink

parts.note: AB stands for able seaman, so sailors are ABs
taken as written

explanation.surface: Seamen have ended up in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the drink' suggests falling overboard, but 'drink' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinthe is a strong green aniseed-flavoured spirit.

clue.text: Short headed in a photo finish?

definitions.text: Short headed in a photo finish?

parts.words: Short headed in a photo finish?
parts.note: beaten by a short head in a close race is being beaten narrowly right at the finishing line

explanation.surface: A racehorse loses by a short head in a photo finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short headed' is a racing term: beaten by a short head, a very narrow margin.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means beaten narrowly at the last moment, like a horse caught on the line.

clue.text: See 8
Deportee from a French island

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of, so from
ile is French for island

explanation.surface: Someone is deported from an island in France.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile is a person banished from their country, as a deportee is.

clue.text: Standard base for a pavement artist

definitions.text: Standard base for a pavement artist

parts.words: Standard base for a pavement artist
parts.note: a standard is a flag, and a pavement artist chalks on the paving slabs, so a paving slab is his base

explanation.surface: A description of the usual surface a street artist draws on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' hints at FLAG, a banner, and the slab is the pavement artist's base.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat paving slab of stone, the usual unit of a pavement.

clue.text: General's sheltered side

definitions.meaning: Robert E. ... was the Confederate general
the side away from the wind

explanation.surface: The general's position is on the protected flank.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert E. Lee led the Confederate army; also the leeward side sheltered from the wind.

clue.text: Self-righteous, he has broken harp I observe

indicators.note: broken signals the harp's letters are smashed into a new order

parts.note: to observe is to see

explanation.surface: A smug man with a smashed harp watches on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-righteous, he' reads as a comment on a character, but together the words define the answer, a sanctimonious man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pharisees, a strict Jewish sect, became a byword for sanctimonious hypocrites.

clue.text: Silver hunt around may come to this

indicators.note: around suggests letters moved about, so silver's symbol and hunt are mixed

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
taken as written

explanation.surface: A search for silver may end in nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a search going round in circles; 'around' instead mixes the silver symbol with the letters of 'hunt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans that come to naught come to nothing, the fate the definition describes.

clue.text: Tea-chest I discover of artistic taste

indicators.note: to discover is to uncover by moving things about, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone opens a tea chest and finds an artistic treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discover' rearranges TEACHEST plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic concerns beauty and the appreciation of art.

clue.text: Cocktail that may go over the bar

definitions.meaning: a long mixed drink of spirits with soda

definitions.text: that may go over the bar
definitions.meaning: a lofted shot or kick passes high above the crossbar

explanation.surface: A drink that might be pushed across the pub counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' suggests the pub, but the second reading is a high ball over a goal's crossbar.
explanation.definitionFit: A whisky and soda served long is a highball; also a ball struck high.

clue.text: Nocturnal creature, yes. You can say that again

indicators.note: an instruction to say the word twice, so it is repeated

parts.note: aye is an old or dialect word for yes

explanation.surface: Agreement with a remark about a night animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You can say that again' is a phrase of emphatic agreement, but here it doubles AYE.
explanation.definitionFit: The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur of Madagascar.

clue.text: Derby winner, possibly, a couple of seasons hence

definitions.text: Derby winner, possibly, a couple of seasons hence

parts.words: Derby winner, possibly, a couple of seasons hence
parts.note: the Derby is for three-year-olds, so a horse one year old could win it two seasons later

explanation.surface: A tip on a future champion racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is the English classic flat race at Epsom, run by three-year-old horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse in its second year, two seasons from being a three-year-old.

clue.text: See 17
Politician left in a mixed state? Spot on!

indicators.note: in puts the politician and left inside the jumble

parts.note: pie is printers' type jumbled together, a mixed state
MP is Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician in confusion is told the remark is spot on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot on!' looks like praise; 'Spot' is the definition. Pie (or pi) is type spilled into a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimple is a small spot on the skin.

clue.text: Welsh banker second in Great Britain and Northern Ireland

indicators.note: in sets the letter for second inside the abbreviation for the country

parts.note: UK is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A Welsh financier is ranked second in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is a crossword word for a river, something with banks; the Usk flows through south Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is a thing with banks, and the Usk is a river in Wales.

clue.text: Engaging enough to persuade several to join

parts.note: to win someone over is to persuade them enough
some means several

explanation.surface: Charming enough to talk several people into joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsome describes charm that attracts people, so it is engaging.

clue.text: Material evidence of QC in camera?

parts.note: something caught in a camera is a shot
a Queen's Counsel is called a silk, from the silk gown worn

explanation.surface: Photographic proof involving a senior barrister in a closed court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in camera' is legal Latin for a private hearing, but here a camera takes a shot of the silk.
explanation.definitionFit: Shot silk is a woven fabric whose colour changes with the light.

clue.text: Measure hour before eight

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A timing just before eight o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Height is a dimension, a measurement of how tall something is.

clue.text: Wrapper put on by one Scotsman in ten seconds flat

indicators.note: in places one and the Scotsman inside the knockout

parts.note: a boxer flat on the canvas for a count of ten is knocked out, a KO
I is the Roman numeral one
mon is a Scots form of man

explanation.surface: A Scotsman throws on a dressing gown in a flash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ten seconds flat' sounds like speed, but it is the count of ten that ends a boxing knockout.
explanation.definitionFit: A kimono is a loose Japanese robe wrapped and sashed round the body.

clue.text: She left the old sea dog for a born swimmer

parts.note: taken as written
Sir Francis Drake, the Elizabethan seafarer

explanation.surface: A woman abandons a weathered sailor for a natural athlete in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The shelduck male is a waterfowl, which swims from birth.

clue.text: He has Dolly in a twist, by George!

definitions.note: the definition is the word standing beside George in a famous name

indicators.note: in a twist means twisted, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation as someone gets a girl named Dolly flustered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' is an exclamation of surprise, but it means the name that stands next to George: David Lloyd George, British Prime Minister 1916-22.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh statesman's surname was Lloyd George, so the first part sits by George.

clue.text: Poems in a classic setting

indicators.note: setting means arranging, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Verse written about a famous scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' rearranges POEMS; the whole clue also says that Epsom is a setting for classics, the Derby and the Oaks, two of England's five classic horse races.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs racecourse in Surrey stages two of the classic races.

clue.text: Brief study in a non-clerical way

indicators.note: in tucks the word for study inside the lay term

parts.note: laic means lay, not of the clergy
to con is to study

explanation.surface: A short course of study done in a secular manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech uses few words, so it is terse.

clue.text: Presiding force for Hepplewhite or Chippendale, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the person who runs a meeting
George Hepplewhite and Thomas Chippendale were famous English furniture makers, men known for their seats

explanation.surface: Was a furniture designer in charge of the board?
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who presides over a meeting; also, read as two words, a maker of seats.

clue.text: Crafty innuendo from an archaeologist?

definitions.meaning: an archaeologist's work is an excavation, here a secret one

explanation.surface: A sneaky barb from a scholar of antiquities.
explanation.definitionFit: A sly dig is a crafty jibe; an archaeologist digs, so a secret excavation is one too.
